newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Congress, United Front try to avoid polls.
newsitem.headline: India's Congress, United Front try to avoid polls.

text.p: Leaders of India's Congress party and caretaker prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda's ousted coalition said on Saturday they wanted to form a new power-sharing agreement to avoid a mid-term election.
"The first priority is to avoid elections," Congress party president Sitaram Kesri told Reuters the day after his party helped to topple Deve Gowda's United Front coalition government.

Deve Gowda was soundly defeated in a vote of confidence in parliament late on Friday, and immediately submitted the resignation of his 10-month centre-left government to President Shankar Dayal Sharma.
Sharma asked Deve Gowda to remain as caretaker prime minister while efforts were made to forge a new governing majority in the hung parliament.

Sitaram Yechury, a member of the United Front's decision-making Steering Committee, told Reuters that Deve Gowda's alliance, comprised of regional, centrist and communist parties, also did not want elections.
"There is an overwhelming demand for a need to avoid elections," Yechury said. "So we are meeting at the United Front to try to form a government."
Senior United Front leaders congregated at the caretaker prime minister's official residence to map strategy ahead of anticipated talks with its ally-turned-foe, Congress.
Congress provoked the fall of Deve Gowda's government by withdrawing its support for the coalition on March 30.
Earlier, Kesri had said he wanted to stake a claim to form a fresh government.
However, when asked on Saturday if he would ask the president for the right to forge a new majority, Kesri said: "That is not the most important issue."

In a sign of the changed circumstances since Friday's vote of confidence, Finance Minister P. Chidambaram abandoned his chauffeur-driven official car and arrived at the meeting behind the wheel of his small sedan.
The common desire to avert elections stemmed from the shared conviction that the second polls in a year would only strengthen the hand of the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

The rightwing party is the largest single group in the 542-member lower house with 162 votes, and held power for 12 days last May before it resigned in the face of certain defeat in a confidence vote.

The BJP has said it would stake a new claim to power only if it were able to muster a majority -- an unlikely prospect given the aversion in the United Front and Congress camps to allying with the Hindu nationalist party.
But fresh elections could put the BJP within striking distance of a majority, according to a recent opinion survey.
With Deve Gowda out of power except in a caretaker capacity, some politicians were expecting an easing of tension between Congress and the United Front.
But it was not clear whether they could dispel the acrimony that has built up over the last two weeks and settle on a common candidate and political programme to avert new elections.
All political formations agreed on Friday to try to approve the 1997/98 (April-March) budget in a special sitting of parliament from April 21 to 23.

The budget plan, which would cut corporate and personal income taxes, has been held hostage to the two-week-old political crisis. Political leaders said there was a strong consensus in favour of approving the budget, but that it would be open to amendment.
